chapter_theme: Honour ranks above profit, fame and survival itself: one abandons even indispensable acts that would lower one, and one who has lost standing is as worthless as fallen hair. The chapter ends by praising those who would rather die than live degraded.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar, reading it as the sequel to the chapter on lineage: not doing what lowers one (961-963), the fault of doing it (964-966), and the excellence of dying for honour (967-970).

961.reading: Even if they are so excellent as to be indispensable, give up things that would diminish you.
961.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes this a deliberate polemic: he says it rejects a Sanskrit rule that one may do degrading things to survive. The verse names no rival.

positions.position: The acts are ones whose omission would mean death, and they must still be refused.
positions.quote: 'இறப்பவரும் வழி இளிவந்தன செய்தாயினும் உய்க' என்னும் வடநூல் முறையை மறுத்து

positions.position: What is given up is wealth and pleasure that would reduce one's nature, however great the amount.
positions.quote: இது பொருளும் இன்பமும் மிகினும், தன்மை குறைவன் செய்யற்க

positions.position: They are obligatory actions, to be avoided if they lessen one's dignity; death is not raised.
positions.quote: கட்டாயமாகச் செய்து தீர வேண்டிய செயல்கள் என்றாலும்கூட

962.reading: Those who want renown and great manliness together won't do unworthy things even for renown.
962.nuance: சீர் is used against itself: renown bought with unworthy acts is not renown. பேராண்மை is explained by Parimelazhagar as a firmness that doesn't falter anywhere, and he takes it here as honour, not prowess.

963.reading: In abundance you must bow, and in slight and shrunken circumstances you must stand tall.
963.nuance: The posture runs against the circumstances: humility when the world would permit pride, and height when the world would press one down. Humility and honour, often seen as rivals, are the same discipline at different times.

964.reading: People who have fallen from their position are like hair that has fallen from the head.
964.nuance: The verse says மாந்தர், people generally, and Parimelazhagar narrows it to the well-born. Nothing about the hair changes when it falls, only its place, so worth is presented as depending on where it stands.

965.reading: Even those like a hill will sink, if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed.
965.nuance: குன்று works four ways: hill, sinking, lowering, and the tiny red seed குன்றி. The sound itself demonstrates how little separates the great from the small.

966.reading: It brings no praise and doesn't carry one to the gods' land: why then go and stand behind those who scorn you?
966.nuance: The argument is from utility, not pride: it weighs both possible rewards and finds neither.

positions.position: Heaven is a real reward that this conduct fails to gain.
Heaven is non-existent, and the line asks rhetorically whether it could be obtained this way.

967.reading: Rather than live by following those who don't accept you, it is better to be called ruined in that very condition.
967.nuance: கெட்டான் means ruined and can mean dead. Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar take death, while Manakkudavar stays with the word. Parimelazhagar says this replies to someone who would still go for wealth and survival. The verse's சொல் is about what is said of a person, so reputation is the stake.

968.reading: When greatness comes to be stripped of its dignity, is a life nursing the flesh a medicine?
968.nuance: The commentators complete the question: medicine against dying. Since death will come anyway, living on buys nothing. ஊன் reduces the body to meat, which Parimelazhagar notes is what a person is after honour goes.

969.reading: Those who are like the yak that won't live once its hair is gone give up their lives when honour's moment comes.
969.nuance: The image is presented as nature, which Parimelazhagar says shows that this is inborn in them. Kalaignar distances himself with என்பார்கள், 'people say'. The verse doesn't say whether the death is by one's own hand; Kalaignar's next gloss, on 970, does.

positions.position: மானம் வரின் means the point at which honour is won by giving up life.
positions.quote: உயிர் நீக்கத்தான் மானம் எய்தும் எல்லை வரின்

positions.position: மானம் வரின் means when honour is about to be destroyed.

970.reading: The world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who won't live when disgrace comes.
970.nuance: The reward is entirely posthumous and in others' mouths, and ஒளி is the fame that outlasts the person. Parimelazhagar adds heaven by citing Purananuru, which reverses 966's point only in appearance, since there heaven was what degrading service failed to earn.

links.note: 131 says that conduct must be guarded above life. 969 and 970 turn that ranking into an actual death, and show what the abstract comparison costs.

961 gives up even what is indispensable if it would lower one. 1028 warns that a man who is idle and stands on honour will destroy the family he should be building. Honour is the highest thing in one chapter and a hazard in another.

Hair appears at both ends of a value scale in the same chapter. Fallen hair is the worthless thing that a degraded person becomes, and the yak's one lost hair is what can't be survived. The first image is about how others see you, the second about how you see yourself.

Both look at a death through those left behind. 780's soldier dies so that his patron's eyes fill and such death is worth begging for, and 970's man of honour is worshipped by the world. Honour and the warrior ethic share one structure.
125 says bowing is good for all and an added wealth for the rich. 963 keeps the second half and reverses the first for the poor: they are told to stand tall, not to bow.

source_issues: 963: Parimelazhagar's text is truncated and begins partway through his gloss, with no treatment of பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்.
962: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray digit 3.
967: Pope's gloss adds 'in his usual state' for அந்நிலையே and 'died'; the Tamil has கெட்டான்.
968: Pope's couplet says 'as nectar sweet', while his gloss says 'remedy against death'; the Tamil has மருந்து, and only the commentators add death.
